title: Integer to English Words
statement:
Spell a non-negative integer in English using the short scale, with every word in Title Case and single spaces between words. Groups of three digits are followed by the scale word 'Thousand', 'Million' and so on, a hundreds digit is followed by 'Hundred', and the value zero is written as 'Zero'. Values from eleven to nineteen are single words, values from twenty upwards combine the tens word and the units word, groups whose value is zero are skipped entirely, and no leading, trailing or doubled spaces may appear in the answer.

For example, 0 is 'Zero', 115 is 'One Hundred Fifteen', 1001 is 'One Thousand One' and 10000 is 'Ten Thousand'.

Constraints: `0 <= num <= 10000`.

constraints: Inputs are JSON-serializable values satisfying the bounds stated above.
hints: Write down the words for one through nineteen and for the multiples of ten first; those two tables cover any two digit value.
Split the number into groups of three digits from the right, because every group is read in exactly the same way and only the scale word after it changes.
Handle the tens digit before the units digit, and when the tens digit is 1 the units digit is consumed by the teen word.

editorial.approach: The brute force walks the digits from the least significant end and tracks the position inside the current group of three, assembling each group word by attaching the hundreds part, then the tens part, and finally prepending the finished group with its scale name to the growing output string. Repeated string concatenation on that growing output makes it O(d^2) in the number of digits d. The optimal solution slices the number into groups of three digits from the right, renders each group once with two small lookup tables, and joins the rendered groups with their scale names.
editorial.why_optimal: Any correct spelling emits a constant number of words per digit, so Omega(d) output is unavoidable and one pass over the digits is enough, which the chunked version does in O(d) time with O(d) characters of output. Because the constraint caps num at 10000, at most five digits and two scale names are ever reachable, which keeps both implementations fast in practice while still exercising the grouping logic.
editorial.pitfalls: Forgetting that 11 to 19 are single words while 21 is two, which produces 'Ten One' where 'Eleven' belongs. Printing an empty string for zero instead of 'Zero'. Emitting the scale word for a group whose value is zero, which is what keeps 10000 from turning into 'Ten Thousand Thousand'. Leaving a doubled or trailing space after 'Hundred' or between groups. Using integer division on the wrong digit, for instance taking the hundreds digit after the tens digit has already consumed the remainder.
